# The argument, in four infographics

Four one-page summaries of this site's argument, made for LinkedIn from the text of these pages. Each is shown here with **the page it draws on** and **the caveat this site would attach** — because a one-pager has to leave the counter-case out, and this site's rule is that the counter-case travels with the claim. Click any image for the full-size version.

> **Provenance.** Generated with ChatGPT from the text of this site and posted on LinkedIn by the author in September 2026. The quotes on them are the author's; where an image signs a quote *"Sgit"*, read *Dinis Cruz*. Released, like everything here, under CC BY 4.0.

## 1 · Open source is a business model

[![Infographic: Open Source Is a Business Model. Five proven commercial models — hosted/SaaS (GitHub, GitLab, MongoDB), support and services (Red Hat, SUSE, Canonical), enterprise editions (Elastic, Confluent, HashiCorp), marketplace and ecosystem (WordPress, Shopify, VS Code), dual licensing (Elastic, Redis, MariaDB) — and the open source flywheel: community contributes, better software, business sustains it, greater adoption.](../assets/infographics/open-source-is-a-business-model.png)](../assets/infographics/open-source-is-a-business-model.png)

**What it summarises.**[The position](../views/index.md): open source is not charity, it is a way to create value, and there are five well-worn ways to make it pay — hosting, support, enterprise editions, a marketplace, dual licensing. **The page underneath it** is ["technology is not the moat"](../views/index.md#not-the-moat): every one of those five models sells something you have to keep being good at — quality, services, new versions, certification — which is exactly where the site says the commercial line belongs.

> **The caveat this site attaches.** Three of the names on those cards — **Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis** — are also the relicensing cases [the survivability page](../survivability/index.md) catalogues, and MongoDB went SSPL. The models work; what decided whether the code stayed open was not the model but **the copyright structure** — a single corporate holder with a CLA, in every case. So read the cards with [the stress test](../survivability/stress-test.md) in hand, and note that VS Code — the marketplace example — is [the open-core page's strongest example of the model done well, and of its cost](../views/open-core.md). And the flywheel's first spoke, *"community contributes"*, is the one the site is most careful about: the position is that [open source is the right strategy even with zero contributions](../views/index.md#zero-contributions).

## 2 · Why open source is the best commercial strategy for GenAI startups

[![Infographic: Why Open Source is the Best Commercial Strategy for GenAI Startups. Six commercial advantages — faster adoption, community multiplier, industry credibility, lower customer acquisition costs, ecosystem and integrations, sustainable revenue models. It is working for GenAI leaders: Meta (Llama), Mistral AI, Databricks (MLflow), Hugging Face (Transformers), Red Hat. A flywheel for long-term success. Quote: for GenAI startups, open source is the ultimate go-to-market strategy.](../assets/infographics/genai-startups-commercial-strategy.png)](../assets/infographics/genai-startups-commercial-strategy.png)

**What it summarises.** The founder-facing version of the argument: open source removes friction, builds credibility where safety and alignment matter, turns users into the sales channel, and can be monetised through support, hosting, enterprise features and dual licensing without giving up the community. **The page underneath it** is [Owning the code, or opening it](../founders/index.md) — the walk-through of what copying you would actually cost an incumbent, and the pitch it produces: *"You can take it. It will cost you that. Or you can pay me, and have it next week."*

> **The caveat this site attaches.****Llama and Mistral are open-weight models**, and [the agents page is precise about the difference](../agents/index.md#training) between that and open source AI under the OSI's definition — the distinction a browser vendor is now betting on. The strategy argument holds either way; the vocabulary matters when the buyer is a regulator. Two more things a one-pager has to leave out: [the cost argument has a limit](../founders/index.md#settle) — slowness is the moat, so it only protects you from slow competitors — and the "$40B+" figure is a press valuation, which is why [it appears on this site only here, labelled as such](../history/numbers.md).

## 3 · We can't have sovereignty without open source companies and Creative Commons ontologies

[![Infographic: We Can't Have Sovereignty Without Open Source Companies and Creative Commons Ontologies. A native startup is one acquisition away from losing sovereignty: promising local startup, acquisition, loss of control. Open source companies change the equation: durable sovereignty, local ecosystems, strategic independence, shared innovation. The open stack for a sovereign future: applications and services on open source companies on Creative Commons ontologies. Why this matters for the UK and EU.](../assets/infographics/sovereignty-open-source-companies-cc-ontologies.png)](../assets/infographics/sovereignty-open-source-companies-cc-ontologies.png)

**What it summarises.**[Sovereignty requires open source](../views/sovereignty.md), in its four steps — and the one most often missed, that [the schemas matter as much as the code](../views/sovereignty.md#step2), which is what the *Creative Commons ontologies* layer is: open, structured knowledge that no acquisition can move. **The page underneath it** is step four: [company nationality is not sovereignty, because acquisitions move it](../views/sovereignty.md#step4) — the same mechanism as a single copyright holder relicensing, at the scale of a country.

> **The caveat this site attaches.** Open source is **necessary and nowhere near sufficient** — that is the first row of [the sovereignty page's own table of objections](../views/sovereignty.md#counter), and it lands fully. Having the source of a stack you cannot operate is sovereignty on paper. The capability to run and repair it still has to be bought, which is [the villagers argument](../views/villagers.md), and nobody currently funds the walked exit path, which is [the sovereignty-bounties proposal](../funding/index.md#bounties). The infographic says *"one acquisition away"*; the site adds *"and one SLA away"*.

Why sgit matters for all my startups. A virtuous cycle.](../assets/infographics/my-strategy-open-foundations.png)](../assets/infographics/my-strategy-open-foundations.png)

**What it summarises.**[The author's own strategy](../about/index.md): the principles, the sgit layer every company builds on, the four companies, and the two ecosystem projects — [sgraph.ai](https://sgraph.ai) and NFRs. **The page underneath it** is the about page's claim that the strongest evidence for the argument is that [the author runs companies on it](../about/index.md#open), in the open, investor materials included.

> **The caveat this site attaches.** This one is a strategy statement from the person whose strategy it is, so it gets the treatment [the about page gives itself](../about/index.md#interests): the interest is declared, and the two things that keep it honest are that the history is checkable without trusting the author and that [the stress test is run on his own estate](../survivability/self-audit.md), in public, with the result published.
